rationale: B wins because it turns the weak spots in the announcement into story machinery instead of just listing them as caveats. Its "Databricks graded its own model, and that is the part enterprises should check" is a real accountability angle; A's "Why would a company chasing an IPO give away its flagship AI model?" reaches for tension by smuggling in "flagship" and overcooking a vague IPO signal. A is useful, but B is cleaner, sharper, and less likely to hand a reporter the knife.
gaps_in_A: "The $3B ARR disclosure" is sloppy. The update says annualized revenue, not ARR; a markets reporter will care about that distinction.
"flagship AI model" is invented. The facts say a new foundation model, not flagship, core, or material to revenue.
"company chasing an IPO" overstates "signaled an eventual IPO without a date." That is a signal, not a chase, and certainly not a filing window.
It buries the best skepticism. "the only numbers supplied are the company's own" is treated as a proof caveat, when self-benchmarking could have been its own accountability angle.
gaps_in_B: "would rather host a model than call one" assumes hosted or on-prem deployment. The update gives open license and fine-tuning on own data, not deployment architecture.
"open weights mean third parties can begin reproducing them immediately" goes a step beyond the supplied fact of an open license. Likely, but not proven in the update.
"gives away for free" should be tightened to open-sources until the license and commercial terms are known. Free is a claim, not a vibe.
"every markets reporter has already written the 'when will they file' piece" is plausible PR judgment, but it is asserted too broadly without evidence.
